source_read: PMC HTML, PMC13179047 (NIH author manuscript of the published article; full text read in own browser tab: abstract, introduction, methods, results incl. Tables 1-3, practice section, guidelines, limitations, highlights, funding and interests). Figure 1 (PRISMA diagram) not read as an image; its numbers are given in Results 3.1. Supplement (search strings) not read. None of the 14 primary studies was read.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim keeps to the review's descriptions and its limitations, not to its highlights and guidelines, which say music reduces dissociation and anxiety, boosts tolerability, reduces sedative load and is known to promote positive outcomes in ketamine therapy.
claims.note: All counts checked: 14 records (9 + 5; flow 863 - 358 = 505, 505 - 468 = 37, 9 included; 1,413 - 222 = 1,191, 1,191 - 1,186 = 5); searches to December 2023; no appraisal of included studies is described. Kim et al.: 46 children, 23 + 23, recordings musical in 12, non-musical in 8, mixed in 3. Of the nine combination studies, six report favourable results (five with comparison groups plus one case report), Kumar no effect on emergence reactions, Ambesh more dreams or emergence reactions with no unpleasant dreams against 10 controls, Kudoh no music-free group: 'in most of them' holds. Four wording points: (1) 'the only one with a comparison group' - the review's Table 1 says the Breeksema interview study had a control group but did not state how many listened to music; 'the only one that compared music with no music' would match the source exactly; (2) the magnitude says 'against a blank recording', but Kim's control children wore headphones and heard no recording (the statement says this correctly; 'blank soundtrack' was the Patil control); (3) 'one stopped using music' follows Table 1, while the review's text (3.2.1) says some participants felt music kept them tethered; (4) one of the nine combination studies was air medical transport rather than a procedure. The review's abstract and introduction say the extant studies include healthy volunteers, but none of the 14 included studies did (Tables 1 and 2), which supports 'all in clinical settings'.

anchors.locator: 2.0 Methods > 2.1 Protocol and Registration (1st paragraph); 2.2 Information Sources and Search Strategy (1st to 3rd paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: PRISMA-ScR scoping review with an a priori protocol on OSF. Librarian-built search of Embase, PsycInfo/PsycArticles, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science, English only, no date limit, completed November 2022 and updated December 2023; Google Scholar (Publish or Perish) February 2023, updated December 2023, screened directly at full text.

anchors.locator: 2.3 Eligibility Criteria (1st and 2nd paragraphs); 2.4 Selection of Sources of Evidence; 2.5 Data Collection Process, Data Items, and Synthesis of Results (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Any population, dose, route and music type; case studies included; non-music sounds, music videos, recreational settings, animal studies, conference material and reviews excluded. Two reviewers screened and extracted independently; an inductive thematic synthesis of the five ketamine-alone studies. No risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of the included studies is described.

anchors.locator: 3.0 Results > 3.1 Selection of Sources of Evidence (1st to 4th paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: Databases: 863 records, 358 duplicates, 505 screened, 468 excluded, 37 at full text, 9 included. Google Scholar: 1,413 records, 222 duplicates, 1,191 at full text, 1,186 excluded, 5 included. Total 14: five on music with ketamine or esketamine alone, nine with ketamine combined with other substances.

anchors.locator: Table 1, row Kim et al., 2010; 3.2.3 Music's Impact on Pediatric Anxiety (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: 46 children having cardiac catheterisation under IV ketamine: 23 heard recordings of their mothers singing, talking or praying through headphones (musical in 12, non-musical in 8, mixed in 3), 23 controls wore headphones and heard no recording. Recording group: lower preoperative anxiety, fewer emergence reactions, less emergence agitation. The only ketamine-alone study with a quantitative music versus no-music comparison.

anchors.locator: Table 1, rows Pereira et al., 2021 and Greenway et al., 2021; 3.2.2 Mitigating Dissociation and Anxiety (1st paragraph); 3.2.4 Enhancing Tolerability and Treatment Outcomes (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Pereira: one 64-year-old woman with major depression on intranasal esketamine; music of her choice from her phone helped with dissociative symptoms, confusion and anxiety; no control. Greenway: two patients with bipolar I depression on IV ketamine; preferred music from the second infusion on improved tolerance of dissociation; the review notes the patients may simply have become accustomed to the infusions; no control.

anchors.locator: Table 1, rows Breeksema et al., 2022 and Mollaahmetoglu et al., 2021; 3.2.1 Music as a Distraction/For Noise Reduction and as an Aid to Internal Exploration (1st paragraph); 3.2.5 Adding More Depth to the Experience (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Breeksema: 17 people with treatment-resistant depression on oral esketamine, qualitative; music blocked distractions, anchored them to reality and aided internal exploration; Table 1: one participant stopped using music because it kept him attached to the outside world (text: some participants felt tethered); Table 1 also says there was a control group without saying how many listened to music. Mollaahmetoglu: 12 people with severe alcohol use disorder given IV ketamine in a trial; all 12 who listened to music heard distortions of speed and pitch, experienced as positive or negative depending on their state; no music control.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (all rows); 3.3 Studies Examining Music and Ketamine in Conjunction with Other Substances (1st to 8th paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: Nine studies with other sedatives, analgesics or anaesthetics: de Araujo Azi (n = 107, less sedation and anxiety; text and table assign the 53/54 group sizes the other way round), Patil (n = 50 children, no extra sedatives in 18/25 with music vs 5/25), Karakul (n = 33, lower pain, fear and anxiety), Bay (n = 100, lower anxiety and pain), Gochenour (n = 490, air medical transport, lower doses and pain), Sudore (one case, relaxing), Kumar (n = 50, randomised, no unpleasant dreams and felt better, no effect on emergence reactions), Ambesh (n = 80, more dreams in Table 2 or emergence reactions in the text with music, no unpleasant dreams with music against 10 controls), Kudoh (n = 40, both groups heard music, no difference in evoked potentials).

anchors.locator: 5.0 Limitations and Future Directions (1st and 2nd paragraphs); 4.0 Guidelines (1st bullet); Table 3
anchors.extracted: Review's limitations: few studies, no associations could be investigated and no conclusions drawn; English only; most studies concern anaesthesia; ketamine-alone studies small, without quantitative analyses, robust statistics or proper controls. Guidelines: studies of ketamine for neuropsychiatric disorders have not systematically examined music. Table 3: 'lack of information' for music with subanaesthetic ketamine.

anchors.locator: Highlights; 3.3 (last paragraph); 3.4 Thoughtful Implementation (2nd paragraph); 4.0 Guidelines (2nd bullet); Abstract; 1.0 Introduction (4th paragraph)
anchors.extracted: The review's summaries go beyond its evidence: highlights say music reduces dissociation and anxiety and boosts tolerability with ketamine alone, and reduces sedative load in combination studies; a guideline calls calming instrumental music known to promote positive outcomes in ketamine sessions. Abstract and introduction say studies were done in healthy volunteers, but none of the 14 included studies involved healthy volunteers.

key_findings.correction: Replace 'only one had a control group' with: only one compared music with no music (Kim et al., 2010); the review's Table 1 records a control group for the Breeksema interview study without saying how many listened to music, and the other three had no control group. The rest of the finding (46 children; 12/8/3 recordings; outcomes; the other four studies) is confirmed.

key_findings.note: 'One participant stopped' follows Table 1; the review's text (3.2.1) says some participants felt music kept them tethered to the outside world.
One of the nine was air medical transport (Gochenour), not a procedure.

reporting_issues.note: Sex counts agree (43M/10F + 33M/21F = 76M/31F); only the group labels are swapped.
Table 1 also says there was a control group in that study; see the correction to key finding 2.

Reference list titles checked: Kaelen 2015 (LSD and emotional response to music) and 2016 (LSD and music-induced imagery). My own reading of Kaelen 2018 in this round confirms that all patients heard music and no brain measures were taken.
The PMC page text ends with the references; no supplementary-materials section is listed.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high under the editors' review checklist (none-applicable), following the two high domains: no appraisal of included studies, and benefits stated as findings in the highlights and recommendations.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: highlights, 3.3, 3.4 and a recommendation state effects the limitations say cannot be concluded.

missed: The abstract and introduction (4th paragraph) say the extant studies include healthy volunteers, but none of the 14 included studies did (Tables 1 and 2); every included study was in patients in clinical or trial settings.
Minor: Table 1 (Pereira row) says 'open-label ketamine' for the phase after the double-blind esketamine period, apparently a slip for esketamine.
